summary: For 5–7 year olds, introduce astronauts as real people with a job who travel to space in rockets. The aim is factual awareness plus wonder: knowing what an astronaut is and a few vivid, concrete things they do (float, eat from pouches, sleep strapped in, do experiments, look down on Earth, and wear a spacesuit to go outside), that humans walked on the Moon during Apollo, and that astronauts today live and work on the International Space Station orbiting Earth. Lead with the memorable microgravity details that make 'working in space' concrete. State the reason for floating simply and honestly — astronauts and the Station are falling around Earth together in orbit — and avoid saying 'there is no gravity in space', the key misconception to steer around.
misconceptions: Astronauts float because 'there is no gravity in space' (they float because they are in continual free fall / orbit around Earth — state simply, don't entrench the no-gravity idea)
Astronauts can breathe normally in open space / don't need a spacesuit (the suit provides air and protection; space has no air)
The Moon landings and living on the ISS are the same thing / happening now on the Moon (Apollo walked on the Moon in the past; the ISS orbits Earth today — no one currently lives on the Moon)
Astronauts fly to the stars or other planets routinely (so far people have only travelled to the Moon and to orbit around Earth)
An astronaut is a kind of superhero rather than a trained person doing a job (they are scientists/pilots/engineers who train for years)

activities.title: Explore a Space Station scene
steps: Look at a cutaway scene of life on the International Space Station and point to or tap each part to hear one short, true fact.

Find and name the astronaut floating inside the Station in ordinary clothes; notice the floating blob of water drifting instead of pouring down, the sleeping bag zipped and strapped to the wall, dinner coming from a pouch, and the big window looking down on the blue curve of Earth.
Find a separate labelled spacesuit (helmet and gloves) and learn it is what astronauts put on to go OUTSIDE the Station — it gives them air and protection because space has no air.
Look at a rocket beside the scene ('this is how they get up there') and a real Apollo Moon-walk photo ('people once walked on the Moon').
Ask or explore 'why does everything float?' and check the answer: the astronaut and everything around them are falling around the Earth together, which is why it all floats.
activities.insight: Astronauts are people doing a job in space; living in microgravity looks surprising (floating food, sleeping on a wall), floating happens because they are in continual free fall around Earth — not because gravity has vanished — and the spacesuit is for going outside where there is no air.

activities.title: Ask an astronaut (in-role conversation)
steps: Pose simple questions to a friendly astronaut character in role on the ISS — spoken aloud or chosen from picture-button prompts ('sleeping', 'eating', 'floating', 'the Moon') so pre-readers can still ask.
Ask what floating feels like, how they sleep, what they eat, and what they can see out the window.
Follow up with their own wonder questions and listen to short, concrete, awe-filled answers.
activities.insight: Astronauts are real people with experiences a child can ask about; turning facts into a back-and-forth conversation is intended to deepen engagement and draw out the experiential 'what it is like to live in space' detail.

activities.title: Check and sort the key facts
steps: Answer 'What is an astronaut?' (a person who travels to space).
Match astronaut kit to its job: sealed helmet → keeps in the air the astronaut breathes (the suit's backpack supplies the air), suit → protection for going outside.
Point to the picture that shows where astronauts live and work now (the ISS orbiting Earth).
Say whether people live on the Moon today (no — Apollo astronauts visited in the past; astronauts now live on the Station near Earth).
activities.insight: The landmark facts — astronaut = person who goes to space, people walked on the Moon in the past, the ISS is where they live and work now — can be recalled and distinguished.

activities.title: Playful 'life in space' and a guided float (optional extensions)
steps: In a small drag activity, catch floating food blobs or pack an astronaut into a sleeping bag strapped to the wall, then say why things drift instead of falling.
Optionally take a gentle guided float through the Station's modules, stopping at tappable spots (floating, sleeping, eating, the window) and naming what astronauts do there.
activities.insight: Microgravity can be made playful and spatial; doing and moving through the scene reinforces that there is 'no up or down' and that astronauts float because everything is falling around Earth together.

checkQuestion: On the Space Station, astronauts float around inside instead of standing on the floor. Why do you think they float? And is the Space Station far away out among the stars, or is it close to Earth going around it? Tell me WHY.
checkAnswer: Astronauts float because they and the Station are both falling around Earth together (going round and round in orbit), NOT because gravity has vanished — there is still gravity up there. The Space Station is quite close to Earth, circling around it, not far away among the stars. Astronauts are people who travel to space in rockets; some walked on the Moon long ago during the Apollo missions, and today astronauts live and work on the Space Station as it orbits Earth.
